title: Snack Budget Mission
subject: math
learningGoal: Add small amounts of money and decide whether a choice fits a budget.
realWorldHook: Grown-ups plan what to buy so they don't spend more than they have. Today your child plans a pretend picnic.

materials.householdSubstitution: Any scrap paper, the back of an envelope, or a whiteboard

materials.item: Five small price cards you write yourself
materials.householdSubstitution: Sticky notes or torn paper squares

noPurchaseRoute: Write the five pretend prices on scraps of paper. Nothing needs to be bought; all prices are made up.
parentPreview: Your child gets $10 of pretend money and five snack cards with made-up prices. They add prices to find combinations that fit. You ask questions; they do the adding. Prices are fictional and this never involves your real household spending.

parent.parentSays: Imagine we're packing a picnic and we have exactly $10 of pretend money. What snacks would you want to bring?
parent.whyThisWorks: Starting with their own wishes makes the maths feel like their plan, not a worksheet.

child.screen: We have $10 of pretend money for a picnic!
child.readAloudText: We have ten pretend dollars for a picnic. Tap I'm ready when you are.

parent.parentSays: Write five price cards together (apple 2, banana 1, crackers 3, juice 4, cheese 5 dollars) and lay them where you can both see.
parent.whyThisWorks: Writing the prices themselves helps your child hold the numbers in mind.

child.screen: Help make the snack cards: apple $2, banana $1, crackers $3, juice $4, cheese $5.
child.readAloudText: Apple two dollars. Banana one dollar. Crackers three. Juice four. Cheese five.

parent.parentSays: Pick three snacks you'd like. Add them up out loud. What's the total?
parent.whyThisWorks: Adding three small numbers invites strategies like making 5 or counting on from the biggest.

child.screen: Apple + crackers + juice. How much is that altogether?
child.readAloudText: Apple, crackers and juice. How many dollars altogether?

parent.parentSays: Does that fit in our $10? How much would be left over? Could we swap something to use the money better?
parent.whyThisWorks: Comparing to the budget and finding what's left is the start of subtraction as 'difference'.

child.screen: Is $9 enough room in our $10? Is there money left?
child.readAloudText: Does nine dollars fit inside ten dollars?

parent.parentSays: Tell me how you worked out the total. Did you start with the biggest number? Did you make a ten?
parent.whyThisWorks: Explaining a strategy helps it stick and shows you how they think, not just the answer.

child.screen: Tell your grown-up how you worked it out.
child.readAloudText: Tell your grown-up how you added the prices.

parent.parentSays: Ask the two check questions below. Give your child time to think, then note how each one went.

child.readAloudText: Two quick questions. Your grown-up will read them.

parent.parentSays: What was the trickiest part? What would you buy with $10 next time?

child.readAloudText: You planned a whole picnic. Well done exploring money.

expectedResponses: Strategies: start with the biggest price, make 5 or 10, count on

misconceptions.signal: Says '3' because there are three snacks, instead of adding the prices.
misconceptions.supportiveNextQuestion: What does the number on each card tell us? Let's add those numbers instead of counting cards.

misconceptions.signal: Adds only two of the prices or adds one twice.
misconceptions.supportiveNextQuestion: Can you point to each card as you add it, so we know we've counted each price once?

misconceptions.signal: Thinks any total is fine, or that $12 fits in $10.
misconceptions.supportiveNextQuestion: If we only have $10, what happens when the snacks cost $12? Which card could we swap?

checkQuestions.parentAsks: Banana $1, cheese $5 and crackers $3 — how much altogether?

interpretation.clear: Says $9, with or without counting on.
interpretation.partial: Gets close (8 or 10) or needs fingers for every step.
interpretation.not_yet: Counts cards or guesses without adding.

child.readAloudText: Banana, cheese and crackers. How many dollars?

checkQuestions.parentAsks: You have $10 and buy juice for $4. How much money is left?

interpretation.clear: Says $6 and can explain (counting up from 4, or 10 take away 4).
interpretation.partial: Reaches 6 with help or says 5 or 7.
interpretation.not_yet: Adds instead of finding what's left (says 14).

child.screen: You have $10. Juice costs $4. How much is left?
child.readAloudText: You have ten dollars. Juice costs four. How much is left?

extension: Give a $7 budget and ask for the most snacks they can get. Then: is there more than one way?

shorterVersion.description: Skip making cards: say the prices aloud and do one pick plus the check.

accessibilityAdaptations: Use real objects (toys) as snacks if reading is hard.
Let your child count on with fingers or a number line drawn on paper.
Turn on read-aloud on the child device.
